title: 09. Storage, CDN & Data Engineering: Data Archiving
summary: Data archiving is the practice of moving infrequently-accessed data from hot, expensive, fast-tiers of storage (SSD-backed object storage or databases) to cheaper, slower-tiers (Glacier, Azure Archive, Google Coldline)…
objectives: What is the difference between backup, archive, and cold storage?
How do S3 lifecycle policies work, and how do you design them?
What is WORM storage, and why is it required for compliance?
What is the cost trade-off between hot and cold storage, and when does archiving pay off?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Data archiving is the practice of moving infrequently-accessed data from hot, expensive, fast-tiers of storage (SSD-backed object storage or databases) to cheaper, slower-tiers (Glacier, Azure Archive, Google Coldline) governed by lifecycle policies, retention rules, and compliance requirements — accepting retrieval latencies of minutes to hours in exchange for 10–100x lower storage cost per terabyte.

Not all data is accessed equally. A typical e-commerce platform generates terabytes of order records, clickstream events, and product images per month, but the access pattern is brutally skewed: data from the last 30 days is queried constantly (customer service lookups, recommendation refreshes, dashboard queries), data from 30–90 days ago is touched occasionally (quarterly reports, refund disputes), and data older than 90 days is rarely touched but legally required to be retained for 7 years (tax audits, payment-card industry compliance, consumer protection laws). Storing all of this on hot SSD-backed storage is both wasteful — the 95% of data that is never accessed still costs the same per gigabyte as the 5% that is hit constantly — and operationally risky, because bigger hot stores mean slower backups, longer replication, and more capital expenditure. Archiving solves this by introducing tiers of storage with different price-latency trade-offs: hot (millisecond access, ~$23/TB-month on S3 Standard), warm (sub-second access, ~$12.50/TB-month on S3 Standard-IA), cold (minutes to hours retrieval, ~$1/TB-month on S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval), and deep archive (12+ hours retrieval, ~$0.4/TB-month on S3 Glacier Deep Archive).

The real-world example par excellence is Netflix. Netflix streams petabytes of video per day, but each title has a long tail of declining viewership — a new release gets hit constantly for 90 days, then interest drops sharply. Netflix archives completed productions, raw camera footage, and older catalog assets to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, where they sit at $0.00099 per GB-month (about $1/TB-month), only to be retrieved if a remaster or re-encode is needed. The savings are enormous: 1 PB of cold footage costs ~$1,000/month on Glacier Deep Archive vs ~$23,000/month on S3 Standard, a 23x reduction. Retrieval latency is 12 hours, but for archive purposes that is fine — the workflow is "submit retrieval request in the morning, get a notification by evening, download overnight." Banks apply the same pattern to transaction records: by regulation (SEC Rule 17a-4, SOX, PCI-DSS), they must retain 7 years of trade and transaction data, but anything older than 18 months is queried only during audits or investigations. Archiving that historical layer to Glacier cuts the storage bill by 95% with negligible operational impact.

The core mechanism is **lifecycle policies** — declarative rules attached to a bucket or table that say "transition objects to Standard-IA after 30 days, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days, to Glacier Deep Archive after 180 days, and delete after 2,555 days (7 years)." These rules are evaluated daily by the storage service and execute automatically, no application code required. The trade-offs are: (1) **retrieval latency** — Standard returns in milliseconds, Glacier Flexible in 1–5 minutes, Glacier Deep in 12 hours, so any archive access must be planned; (2) **retrieval cost** — Glacier charges per-GB retrieval fees ($0.03/GB for standard, $0.10/GB for expedited) plus a per-request fee, so retrieving a large archive back to hot is expensive; (3) **early deletion fees** — Glacier Deep Archive requires 180 days of storage before deletion is free, so deleting early incurs a prorated charge; (4) **lock compliance** — for regulated industries, S3 Object Lock and Glacier Vault Lock provide WORM (Write Once Read Many) guarantees that even root admins cannot bypass, preventing premature deletion during audits.

A second major driver is **compliance retention**. HIPAA requires 6 years of medical records, FINRA requires 7 years of broker communications, GDPR mandates data minimization but also mandates deletion on request — and these regulations often conflict (you cannot delete user data that the tax authority requires you to keep). The archive tier becomes the system of record for compliance: a searchable metadata index (often Elasticsearch or Athena on Glue) points to immutable archive copies, and legal holds freeze specific objects until released. Modern architectures combine cold storage with a metadata layer that remains queryable, so analysts can ask "how many customers in region X had event Y in 2019?" without restoring the raw data — the answer comes from pre-computed aggregates or a metadata index, and only when the actual records are needed is a restore initiated.

The architecture choice is rarely "archive or not" but "where to draw the tier boundaries." Data warehouses partition by date and move old partitions to cheaper storage; databases implement native tiering (MongoDB Online Archive, Postgres with tablespace on cold disk); object stores use lifecycle policies on buckets. The right design matches the access pattern: archive aggressively when access drops off a cliff (Netflix-style long tail), archive conservatively when access decays gradually (a financial dashboard that still gets quarterly queries for 7 years), and never archive the metadata index that tells you what to retrieve.

Application writes data (order records, video assets, log events) to S3 Standard — hot tier, millisecond access, full price. 2. A lifecycle policy attached to the bucket evaluates objects daily and transitions them: after 30 days to Standard-IA (warm), after 90 days to Glacier Flexible Retrieval (cold), after 180 days to Glacier Deep Archive. 3. Each transition reduces cost 5–25x and increases retrieval latency proportionally — the policy matches the access pattern decay curve. 4. When the application needs archived data, it submits a restore request; Glacier stages the object into a temporary S3 Standard bucket after the tier's retrieval latency (1 min to 12 hr), then the application reads it. 5. Compliance Vault Lock and Object Lock enforce WORM on cold/deep tiers — legal holds prevent deletion even by root admins, satisfying SEC/HIPAA/FINRA retention rules. 6. After the retention period (e.g., 7 years), the lifecycle policy deletes the object automatically, or permanent lock keeps it forever.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
"""
Data Archiving Lifecycle Simulator

Mocks a tiered storage system with lifecycle policies, retrieval,
and compliance lock. Demonstrates the cost/latency trade-offs.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from enum import Enum
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

class Tier(Enum):
    HOT = ("S3 Standard", 23.0, 0.001)          # $/TB-mo, retrieval hours
    WARM = ("S3 Standard-IA", 12.5, 0.001)
    COLD = ("Glacier Flex", 1.0, 1/60)           # 1 minute
    DEEP = ("Glacier Deep", 0.4, 12.0)           # 12 hours

@dataclass
class ArchiveObject:
    key: str
    size_gb: float
    created: datetime
    tier: Tier = Tier.HOT
    last_accessed: datetime = field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    legal_hold: bool = False
    vault_locked: bool = False

@dataclass
class LifecycleRule:
    transition_after_days: int
    target_tier: Tier
    delete_after_days: Optional[int] = None

class ArchiveStore:
    def __init__(self, rules: List[LifecycleRule]):
        self.objects: Dict[str, ArchiveObject] = {}
        self.rules = sorted(rules, key=lambda r: r.transition_after_days)

    def put(self, key: str, size_gb: float) -> None:
        self.objects[key] = ArchiveObject(key, size_gb, datetime.now())

    def apply_lifecycle(self, now: datetime) -> List[str]:
        transitions = []
        for obj in self.objects.values():
            age_days = (now - obj.created).days
            for rule in self.rules:
                if age_days >= rule.transition_after_days and obj.tier != rule.target_tier:
                    if obj.vault_locked or obj.legal_hold:
                        continue  # locked objects cannot be deleted but CAN be tiered
                    obj.tier = rule.target_tier
                    transitions.append(f"{obj.key} -> {rule.target_tier.value[0]}")
                if rule.delete_after_days and age_days >= rule.delete_after_days:
                    if not (obj.vault_locked or obj.legal_hold):
                        transitions.append(f"{obj.key} -> DELETED (age {age_days}d)")
                        self.objects.pop(obj.key, None)
                        break
        return transitions

    def restore(self, key: str) -> str:
        obj = self.objects[key]
        latency_hrs = obj.tier.value[2]
        retrieval_cost = obj.size_gb * (0.03 if obj.tier == Tier.COLD else 0.10 if obj.tier == Tier.DEEP else 0)
        obj.last_accessed = datetime.now()
        return (f"Restored {key} from {obj.tier.value[0]} "
                f"in {latency_hrs:.2f}h, retrieval cost ${retrieval_cost:.2f}")

    def monthly_cost(self) -> float:
        return sum(o.size_gb / 1024 * o.tier.value[1] for o in self.objects.values())

    def lock(self, key: str, vault: bool = False) -> None:
        if vault:
            self.objects[key].vault_locked = True
        self.objects[key].legal_hold = True

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rules = [
        LifecycleRule(30, Tier.WARM),
        LifecycleRule(90, Tier.COLD),
        LifecycleRule(180, Tier.DEEP),
        LifecycleRule(2555, Tier.DEEP, delete_after_days=2555),  # 7 yr retention
    ]
    store = ArchiveStore(rules)
    # 100 TB of order records written Jan 1, 2022
    for i in range(100):
        store.put(f"orders/2022/part-{i:03d}.parquet", size_gb=1024)  # 1 TB each

    # Simulate the clock advancing 200 days
    now = datetime(2022, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=200)
    txns = store.apply_lifecycle(now)
    for t in txns[:5]:
        print(t)

    print(f"\nMonthly storage cost (100 TB across tiers): ${store.monthly_cost():,.2f}")
    print(f"(If all stayed on HOT: ${100 * 23:,.2f})")

    # Compliance lock on a specific object
    store.lock("orders/2022/part-000.parquet", vault=True)
    print(f"\n{store.restore('orders/2022/part-050.parquet')}")
```
